claims.text: The proposed predictive approach integrates first-principles defect-inclusive simulations with machine-learning methods.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr contains roughly 1 wt.% oxygen.
The incorporated oxygen creates localized defect structures in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen defects in HfNbTaTiZr may take the form of interstitials or substitutions.
The machine-learning regression will be trained on partial experimental data from selected temperature regimes.
Oxygen and its associated defect structures mediate carrier-scattering processes in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen-associated defects modify electronic transport pathways in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen-associated defects modify phonon transport pathways in HfNbTaTiZr.
Defect-induced scattering and altered local atomic configurations affect the conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicit defect modeling captures electron-phonon interactions and impurity scattering that conventional ideal-crystal models miss.
Learning residual corrections from experimental measurements will improve prediction accuracy.
The defect- and impurity-aware approach will predict conductivity more accurately than analytical models that assume a perfect, defect-free crystal.
The approach may reduce conductivity-prediction error by more than 10% in the 0–200 K regime.
The approach may reduce conductivity-prediction error by more than 10% in the 300–1200 K regime.
The relevant analytical baseline assumes a perfect, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr crystal and ignores the effects of 1 wt.% oxygen.
The approach is applicable only to bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens with oxygen levels similar to 1 wt.%.
The approach may not apply to nanoscale HfNbTaTiZr specimens or outside the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K ranges.
Oxygen clustering or defect interactions outside the modeled configurations could limit prediction accuracy.
The robustness of the machine-learning correction depends on the quality and temperature coverage of the experimental training data.
